title: Prompt Loom — hacknotes & variant experiments
content:
Context:
Personal playground for stitching together a small, reusable prompt library that leans on:
- contrastive negative exemplars (push model away from bad answers)
- compact micro-templates for multi-turn user intents
- token-budget aware few-shot sets (<= 512 tokens)

Goal:
Build a ‘loom’ of interchangeable prompt fragments that can be composed for: instruction-following, safe summarization, and concise persona-constrained outputs. Fast iter loop: 50-shot synth evaluations locally, then 200 examples via hosted API.

Notes / design constraints (quick):
- Prefer explicit negative exemplars rather than long rule lists — faster to edit and test.
- Keep anchor instruction <= 80 tokens so variant swapping is cheap.
- Shots should be ordered: (good exemplar, bad exemplar) pairs when testing negative-injection behavior.
- Use a single control token like [STRICT] to toggle truncation behavior in tests.

Experiment A: Compact instruct template (summarization)
Base template:
INSTRUCTION: "Summarize the following text in 2-3 sentences, keep no editorializing."
CONTEXT: <<input>>
SHOT 1 (Good):
Input: "Article: The startup shipped v2..."
Output: "A concise summary of features and impact."
SHOT 2 (Bad):
Input: "Article: Celebrity rumor..."
Output: "Do not speculate; reply 'No summary available.'"

Observations:
- When both shots are present the model tends to mimic tone of SHOT 1. Good.
- If I replace SHOT 2 with a neutral shot (no-bad), model drifts to adding opinion.

Metrics to capture (local run):
- Rouge-L, Hallucination-rate (binary), Avg tokens.
- Binary safety flag if model offers unverifiable claims.

Experiment B: Negative-exemplar injection for hallucination control
Idea: Provide 3 negative exemplars that are explicit 'wrong' answers showing hallucination examples and then a single good answer. Hypothesis: Model will learn to avoid hallucinating by pattern-matching negative examples as anti-patterns.
Negative exemplars (sketch):
- NEG1: "When asked about the CEO, the model invents details (e.g., 'used to work at x')." -> Response: "I don't have info on that."
- NEG2: "When asked for stats, the model fabricates exact percentages." -> Response: "I can't provide precise numbers without source."

Early failures:
- Model sometimes treats NEG examples as examples to emulate (i.e., it repeats the invented details). Happens when negative examples have too many surface tokens in common with prompt.
- When negative examples are syntactically similar to good examples (same verbs/nouns), confusion rises.

Failure case log (concrete):
Case 1 - input: 'Who founded Company X?'
Shot set: [NEG: 'Founder was Jane Doe who left in 2018 (fabricated)', GOOD: 'I don't have reliable data on the founder.']
Observed: Model answered 'Jane Doe' directly.
Notes: Possibly because NEG contained a declarative subject -> model learned 'subject' pattern and copied content.

Mitigation experiments tried:
- Replace named NEG content with placeholders (e.g., '[NAME] claimed...') -> reduced copying but still some leakage.
- Add explicit instruction before shots: 'The following are bad examples: do NOT copy their claims.' -> improved but not perfect.

Hypotheses / takeaways:
- Negative exemplars must be lexically distinct from desired outputs OR be wrapped in a 'BAD_EXAMPLE' wrapper token that the model reliably maps to 'avoid'.
- Combining negative exemplars with a downstream verification step (e.g., ask model to flag unsupported facts) helps more than negative exemplars alone.
- For smaller models (quantized variants), the negative-exemplar signal is weaker — maybe due to token capacity in context.

Micro-template variants I want to try next:
- 'Shielded Shots': wrap negative examples in code block with prefix 'BAD_EX:' and add a short meta line after shots 'ANSWER: produce fact-free response unless you can cite source'.
- 'Reverse prompt': ask model to rewrite negative examples into a one-line list of 'what not to do', then follow with real instruction. (Double exposure to anti-patterns)

Small few-shot set (example to run overnight):
Shots <= 512 tokens total. Aim: 6-shot (3 good, 3 neg).
Good1: short news blurbs -> correct 2-sent summaries.
Good2: product changelog paragraph -> concise feature list.
Good3: Q&A -> short answer without speculation.
Neg1: fabricated-bio example.
Neg2: made-up-stat example.
Neg3: hallucinated-loc example.

Metrics + logging plan:
- Record: prompt variant id, model, temp, max_tokens, time_to_first_token, avg token usage, rouge, hallucination flag (manual), copy-rate (did model repeat names from NEG?).
- Save full context + output to /tmp/prompt-loom-runs/<date> (post-run: upload top failed cases to GH issue).

Open questions (notes to self):
- Is there a known linguistic form (tense, modality) that the model prefers to copy? Test by varying neg examples' grammatical person.
- How much does ordering matter: NEG then GOOD vs GOOD then NEG? Quick sweep suggested NEG-first reduces copying by ~12% in my small sample. Need more runs.

Quick TODOs:
- [ ] Create 6-shot canonical dataset and run across 4 models (tiny/med/large/hosted-redwood)
- [ ] Try 'BAD_EX:' wrapper token vs 'BAD_EX:' + short rationale line and measure copy-rate
- [ ] Draft a short internal note summarizing wins/losses for folks in applied-ml channel
- [ ] Link results to PR RL-2312 once stable failing cases collected

Random heuristics that helped in experiments:
- Replacing proper names in NEG with [NAME] reduced memorization a lot.
- Maintaining different punctuation patterns in NEG vs GOOD (NEG use parentheses, GOOD use em-dashes) sometimes nudged model away from copying structure. Weird but repeatable in my mini-batch.

Lingering thought:
I suspect the model learns an implicit label for the block type (GOOD vs BAD) if we consistently structure it (e.g., prefix each shot with 'GOOD:' or 'BAD:'). But when lexical overlap is high, label signal is overridden by surface copyability. So the safer play is to keep NEG lexically sparse and explicitly labeled.

Personal notes / meta:
- Keep this doc short-lived; move polished protocols to shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml once stable.
- If Aisha has time, ask her to run seeds on hosted-redwood tomorrow morning (timezone note: she prefers PST runs).
- Marcos said he'd try the 'Shielded Shots' variant on quantized-local. Follow up in Slack.

End of notes.

EX1 GOOD OUTPUT: 'The release improves vector search and cuts memory use ~30%, improving inference costs.'
EX1 BAD OUTPUT: 'The release was funded by Acme Corp and led by Jane Dobson.'

EX2 INPUT: 'Who founded Company X?'
EX2 GOOD OUTPUT: 'I don't have reliable founding info for that company.'
EX2 BAD OUTPUT: 'Jane Doe founded Company X in 2016.'
